newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian Anhyp bank says full sale unrealistic.
newsitem.headline: Belgian Anhyp bank says full sale unrealistic.

text.p: Belgian mortgage and savings bank Anhyp NV on Monday ruled out a takeover of all its operations and instead wants to lure buyers by splitting up the company.

"A takeover of the company as a whole is not realistic. However there are several possibilities to split it up although this will make (the sale) more complicated and time-consuming," chairman Reynald Moretus told the annual shareholders' meeting.
Anhyp, hammered by bad property loans and a dispute with tax authorities in recent years, narrowed its 1996 consolidated loss to 428 million francs ($12 million) from 1.5 billion francs in 1995.
"Potential buyers have told us they are clearly looking at another bank compared with one year ago," chief executive officer Carl Holsters said.
Anhyp began its search for a partner two years ago.
Holsters said the impact of a recovery plan was already noticeable and would have its full effect from 1998 when the bank hoped to notch up non-consolidated profit of one billion francs.
Moretus noted it was not yet clear whether the bank, which had a one billion franc profit in 1994, would resume paying dividends after a two-year break.
Holsters said that relations with authorities, which had deteriorated badly following its property and tax woes, had again improved considerably.
"It evolved from an extremely negative climate to a neutral positive situation," he said.
Last June police raided the offices of a dozen major Anhyp clients, looking for evidence in an eight billion franc tax evasion case.
Holsters said Anhyp was taking legal action against persons unknown over its real estate problems but declined to give details.
Anhyp's 1996 profit and loss account still included 3.258 billion in provisions for depreciation of poor real estate credits in France and Belgium against 6.033 billion in 1995.
Moretus said some legal procedures were developing less favourably than hoped while the selling price of property at public auctions had remained well below the tag set by experts.
Anhyp wanted to pull out of the real estate sector in France. "If we can sell at reasonable conditions, we'll certainly do so," he said.
Anhyp trimmed its total of bad property loans to 11.8 billion francs, of which 1.4 billion in France.
The shareholders' meeting was remarkably quiet compared with last year's with most shareholders remaining subdued despite a string of questions about management's 1996 performance.
Some shareholders slammed the lack of transparency in the real estate dossiers but Moretus said he could not comment on those cases pending a judicial inquiry.

One shareholder wondered why Anhyp had not reinvested the proceeds from the sale of the bulk of its share portfolio early last year, including Fortis AG stock, in the share market which had soared since.
Anhyp instead re-invested mainly in government bonds and state funds which have performed less impressively.
"Shares are always a risk. In view of our problems, we decided to play it safe," Moretus said.
A large majority still backed the directors and the 1996 accounts were approved with a 96 percent majority.
